blocks.text: Regression testing for prompts maintains a suite built from past failures and past successes, running it automatically on every meaningful change to catch when previously working behavior quietly breaks, before that regression ever reaches real users.

This topic covers building a regression suite, running it automatically on every change, catching regressions before they ship, how this differs from benchmarking, and recognizing when an apparent regression is actually an intentional, accepted tradeoff.
1. What Regression Testing Means for Prompts

blocks.alt: Building on benchmarking, regression testing catches previously working behavior that broke

blocks.text: Regression testing specifically checks whether a change has broken something that used to work correctly, rather than measuring overall performance level the way benchmarking does, it asks a narrower, more targeted question, did this specific change introduce a new failure.
2. Building a Regression Suite From Past Failures and Successes

blocks.alt: A past failure now fixed and a past success currently working both get added to the regression suite

blocks.text: This connects directly to prompt debugging, covered in an earlier module, every bug found and fixed becomes a permanent regression test case, ensuring that exact failure never silently returns, every important success case also earns a place in the suite, confirming a future change does not accidentally break something that currently works well.
3. Running the Suite on Every Change

blocks.alt: Every prompt change triggers the regression suite to run automatically

blocks.text: This connects directly to the automated security testing practice covered in an earlier module, the same discipline applies here, running the full regression suite automatically on every meaningful prompt, template, or system configuration change, rather than only occasionally or manually.
4. Catching a Regression Before It Ships

blocks.alt: A regression caught before shipping is compared against one discovered only in production

blocks.text: The entire value of regression testing comes from catching a broken behavior before it ever reaches real users, a regression discovered only after shipping, through user complaints or production monitoring, has already caused real harm, catching it in the regression suite first prevents that harm entirely.

blocks.text: 5. Regression Testing vs Benchmarking

blocks.alt: Benchmarking measures overall performance level, regression testing checks whether anything specific broke

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the previous topic, benchmarking measures overall performance level against a fixed reference, regression testing asks a narrower question, specifically, did this exact change break any previously working, individually important case, the two practices complement each other rather than replacing one another.
6. When an Apparent Regression Is an Accepted Tradeoff

blocks.alt: An intentional, accepted tradeoff is not a genuine regression

blocks.text: Not every change in behavior a regression test flags is actually a genuine problem, a deliberate improvement might intentionally shift behavior on an edge case in a way the team has explicitly decided is an acceptable tradeoff, distinguishing a genuine regression from an intentional, reviewed tradeoff matters, rather than treating every flagged difference as automatically bad.

blocks.title: This is why a human review step still matters even with automation
blocks.content: An automated regression suite flags differences, it does not always know whether a specific difference is a genuine bug or an intentional, accepted improvement, a brief human review of flagged changes keeps this distinction accurate.

blocks.text: 7. Automating Regression Tests Into a Development Workflow

blocks.alt: A regression suite wired into the development workflow runs automatically on every change

blocks.text: The strongest version of this practice wires the regression suite directly into whatever development workflow a team already uses, running automatically whenever a prompt or related configuration changes, exactly the same principle covered for security regression testing in an earlier module, applied here to overall quality.
8. A Worked Regression Testing Example

A team fixes a bug where their classification prompt mishandled a specific edge case input, they add that exact input and its correct expected output as a permanent regression test case, months later an unrelated prompt change accidentally reintroduces the same bug, caught immediately by the regression suite before it ever reaches production.
9. Regression Testing and Golden Datasets

This connects directly to the next topic, golden datasets, the actual curated set of inputs and correct expected outputs a regression suite runs against is often exactly what a golden dataset provides, the next topic covers building and maintaining that reference data itself in depth.
Worked Example

A team without a regression suite ships a prompt improvement intended to make responses more concise, a user later reports that a previously well handled edge case, a multi-part question, now only gets a partial answer, a regression the team had no automated way to catch before shipping.

After adding that specific multi-part question case to a regression suite, and wiring the suite to run automatically on every future prompt change, a similar future change that would have reintroduced this exact issue gets caught immediately, before it ever reaches a real user again.
Common Mistakes

items: Fixing a bug without adding the specific failing case to a permanent regression suite
Running a regression suite only occasionally or manually instead of automatically on every meaningful change
Treating every regression suite flag as an automatic bug without checking whether it is actually an intentional, accepted tradeoff
Confusing regression testing, which checks for specific broken behavior, with benchmarking, which measures overall performance level

blocks.text: Practice

Take a bug you have fixed in a prompt before, or one you could imagine, add the specific failing case and its correct expected output to a small regression suite, and consider how you would wire this suite to run automatically on every future change to that prompt.
Key Takeaway

Regression testing maintains a suite built from past failures and successes, run automatically on every meaningful prompt change to catch when previously working behavior breaks before it ever reaches production, a narrower, more targeted practice than benchmarking, and it requires distinguishing genuine regressions from intentional, accepted tradeoffs.
